Climate Risk Index 2025
=======================

The Climate Risk Index (CRI) ranks countries by the human and economic toll of extreme weather. The latest edition highlights increasing losses and the urgent need for stronger climate resilience and action.

 Share 

[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https://www.germanwatch.org/en/cri&title=Climate%20Risk%20Index%202025 "Share to Facebook (opens in a new window)")[](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=Climate%20Risk%20Index%202025+https://www.germanwatch.org/en/cri "Share to X (opens in a new window)")[](https://wa.me/?text=https://www.germanwatch.org/en/cri "Share to WhatsApp (opens in a new window)")[](https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=https://www.germanwatch.org/en/cri "Share to Linkedin (opens in a new window)")[](mailto:?subject=Climate%20Risk%20Index%202025&body=https://www.germanwatch.org/en/cri "Share to Email")

The Climate Risk Index (CRI), published since 2006, is one of the longest running annual climate impact-related indices. The CRI analyses climate-related extreme weather events’ degree of effect on countries. In doing so, it measures the consequences of realised risks on countries.

This backward-looking index ranks countries by their economic and human impacts (fatalities as well as affected, injured, and homeless) with the most affected country ranked highest.

The CRI visualises such events’ degree of effect at two years before the index’s publication and over the preceding 30 years. The index contextualises international climate policy debates and processes with a view to the climate risk countries are facing. It simplifies the aggregation and understanding of climate-related extreme weather events’ impacts across different regions and time periods. The most strongly affected countries rank highest and should view the CRI results as a warning sign that they are at risk of frequent events or rare and unusual extreme events.

### **CRI 2025 ranking and results highlights**

_Scorching heat, heavy rainfalls, raging wildfires, deadly floods, and devastating storms: The manifestations of extreme weather events have become too common in a new reality worldwide. The Climate Risk Index 2025 relaunch sheds light on inaction’s growing cost. It reveals the mounting human and economic toll._

_From 1993 to 2022, more than **765,000 lives were lost** and **direct economic losses of nearly USD 4.2 trillion** (inflation-adjusted) were recorded, driven by more than **9,400 extreme weather events**. The frequency and intensity of climate-related disasters continue to rise, and these figures underscore the urgent need for climate action._

**For a comprehensive overview of the results, see the full report here.**

### Methodology

The CRI methodology involves analysing extreme weather events’ impacts via three hazard categories: hydrological, meteorological, and climatological. The index visualises these events’ impact on countries both two years prior to publication and over the preceding 30-year period. It draws on data from the EM-DAT international disaster database, World Bank, and International Monetary Fund (IMF). The index considers absolute and relative impacts, using six key indicators: economic loss, fatalities, and affected people – each in absolute and relative terms.

[Download Methodology](https://www.germanwatch.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/Climate%20Risk%20Index%202025%20Methodology.pdf "(opens in a new window)")

Please note: We have received helpful feedback on the readability of the index. Based on this feedback, we have adjusted the annex and added a brief explanation on the method. Therefore, we have uploaded a slightly updated CRI version which you now find online. We will further improve the readability of the index and its annex for its next edition.

![Image 6: KRI-Indikatoren und -Gewichtung in einem Donut-Diagramm](https://www.germanwatch.org/sites/default/files/styles/original_xxl/public/2025-02/CRI%20indicators%20and%20weighting.png.webp?itok=cmCUH8Xa)

Explore an interactive map of the full ranking and results. Click on a country to see how extreme weather events affect it, in terms of the economic and human impacts.

**2022-Map**: Most affected countries in 2022. This map highlights the countries extreme weather events most affected in 2022, based on the impacts on people and on economic loss.

**1993–2022 Map**: Most affected countries in 1993–2022. This map shows the countries extreme weather events most affected from 1993 to 2022, based on the impacts on people and on economic loss.

CRI 2025 key messages
---------------------

1.   The Climate Risk Index (CRI) ranking indicates that, in 1993–2022, **Dominica, China, and Honduras** were the countries most affected by extreme weather events’ impacts.
2.   The ranking shows **Pakistan, Belize, and Italy** as the most affected by extreme weather events’ impacts in 2022.
3.   From**1993 to 2022, 765,000+ people died worldwide and direct losses of nearly USD 4.2 trillion (inflation-adjusted)**directly resulted from 9,400+ extreme weather events.
4.   **Floods, storms, heat waves, and drought** were the most prominent impacts from short- and long-term perspectives. From 1993 to 2022, storms (35%), heat waves (30%), and floods (27%) caused the most fatalities. Floods were responsible for over half of the people affected. Storms caused, by far, the most significant economic losses (56% or USD 2.33 trillion inflation-adjusted), followed by floods (32% or USD 1.33 trillion).
5.   The most affected countries in the long-term index for 1993–2022 can be divided into two groups: (1) Countries most affected by highly unusual extreme events (**e.g. Dominica, Honduras, Myanmar, Vanuatu**) and (2) countries affected by recurring extreme events (**e.g. China, India, the Philippines)**. Climate science clearly shows that climate change increases the risk for both categories and contributes to transforming uncommonly extreme events into continual threats, creating a ‘new normal.’
6.   **The CRI shows that all countries are affected**. Seven of the 10 most affected countries in 2022 belonged to the high-income country group 1. This clearly indicates that, while the coping capacities of high-income countries significantly exceed those of lower-income countries, higher-income countries should also increase their climate risk management. Over the long term, the ranking shows that extreme weather events’ impacts particularly affect Global South countries. With five countries, the lower middle-income group is the largest country group among the 10 most affected countries, including three Small Island Developing States/Least Developed Countries, where coping capacities are significantly lower.
7.   The CRI ranking is based on the best publicly available historical data set on the extreme weather events’ impacts.**Extreme weather events and their impacts are often underreported in Global South countries**because of data quality and coverage challenges and data gaps. As a result, this ranking may less accurately capture these impacts and, therefore, how Global South countries are affected.
8.   **Human-induced climate change affects the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events and leads to widespread adverse climate impacts.** The latest climate science and significantly improved attribution science suggest climate change’s influence on extreme weather events is ‘on the same level of scientific confidence as the statement that human influence has warmed the climate.2
9.   **COP29 failed to deliver an ambitious New Collective Quantified Goal (NCQG) on Climate Finance.** Considering the identified needs, and the great urgency of the climate challenges that developing countries face, the USD 300 billion annually by 2035 can only be seen as the bare minimum response to the escalating climate crisis. The NCQG also failed to include measures to address loss and damage. This gap must be filled as soon as possible. This situation is even more worrying given the extensive gaps in adaptation finance compared with the needs and commitments (even if progress was made). Substantially increased support by high-emitting countries and other polluters is needed for the most vulnerable in addressing climate impacts.
10.   The CRI shows that a **lack of ambition and action in mitigation leads to being strongly affected,** even in high-income countries. It is in the interest of high-income and highly emitting countries to ramp up mitigation action, including higher climate targets and such action’s implementation, with new nationally determined contributions (NDCs), to stay below (or as close as possible to) 1.5°C warming and keep impacts at a manageable scale.

### **FAQ: Understanding the CRI**

 What is the Climate Risk Index (CRI)? 

The CRI is a tool that assesses extreme weather events’ impacts on countries and regions. It ranks countries based on these events’ economic and human impacts two years before publication and over the preceding 30 years. In this way, it measures realised risks’ consequences for countries.

 Why has there been no CRI in recent years? 

The CRI has not been available in recent years because extreme weather event data from the previous data provider was discontinued. The index now uses the EM-DAT international disaster database as its primary data source.

 What’s new in CRI 2025 compared with previous editions? 

In addition to the new database for extreme weather events, a new normalisation technique is applied together with an updated weighting of the indicators.

 How is the CRI different from other indices? 

The CRI measures actual human and economic impacts from extreme weather events. It is a retrospective analysis of realised climate risks.

 How often is the CRI updated? 

The CRI is updated annually, incorporating the latest data on extreme weather events from two years prior. CRI 2025 is an exception, considering the latest available data from 2022.

 How many countries does the CRI cover? 

CRI 2025 covers 171 countries. Some countries are not reflected because of data availability.

 How is the CRI calculated? 

The index examines hydrological, meteorological, and climatological events. Fatalities and economic loss from seven hazard types are included in these categories. A composite score is then generated for ranking countries.

 What data sources are used for the CRI? 

The CRI relies on data from EM-DAT, the World Bank, and the IMF.

 Why do some small countries rank higher than large ones? 

This occurs because small countries often have higher relative fatalities and economic losses, owing to their smaller populations and GDP. Thus, extreme events’ impacts are more significant in relative terms, even if absolute losses are smaller.

 Can the CRI predict future climate impacts? 

No, it cannot. The CRI is a retrospective analysis of past extreme weather-related impacts. However, it serves as a warning for countries likely to face similar events in the future.

 Where does my country rank in the CRI? 

You can access the full list of country rankings in the full report.

 How does the CRI handle data gaps or missing information? 

The CRI relies on the best publicly available databases for generating the results. However, data gaps arise due to variations in data quality and coverage, especially regarding the Global South. Under-representation in research, uneven distribution of meteorological stations, and differing data collection techniques across countries are among the key challenges.

 Can the CRI be used for sub-national or city-level analysis? 

Currently, the CRI is applied only at the national level.

 Does the CRI account for slow-onset climate impacts, such as sea-level rise? 

No, the CRI focuses on sudden-onset extreme weather events, such as floods, storms, and heat waves. Slow-onset changes, such as sea-level rise, are not included.

 Can I suggest improvements for the CRI methodology? 

Yes, the CRI team welcomes feedback and suggestions for methodological improvements. Please submit your ideas via this email: [cri@germanwatch.org](mailto:cri@germanwatch.org "mailto:kri@germanwatch.org").

 How can I stay updated on future CRI releases? 

### Stay informed

Subscribe to our mailing list for updates on our indices (CRI and CCPI).

E-Mail 

 How can I access the CRI database? 

The CRI database will generally be available for research and academic purposes. Please email your request for access to [cri@germanwatch.org](mailto:cri@germanwatch.org "mailto:kri@germanwatch.org") and please provide a clear description of how you plan to use the data. Data availability will be assessed on a case-by-case basis, with preference for academic and public policy research.

 How should I cite the CRI in my research or publication? 

Please cite the CRI 2025 edition as follows:

title: 2025 in climate change - Wikipedia
content:
28 May: the World Meteorological Organization projected a 70% chance that the average global warming for 2025-2029 will be more than 1.5°C, up from 47% in last year’s report for 2024-2028.( [...] 7 March: a study by World Weather Attribution concluded that in a February 2025 heat wave, climate change made extreme heat at least 2°C hotter and at least ten times more likely.(
   21 March: on the first World Glaciers Day (established by the UN General Assembly), the World Meteorological Organization reported that five of the past six years witnessed the most rapid glacier retreat on record, and 2022-2024 witnessed the largest three-year loss of glacier mass on record.( [...] 8 May: NOAA's April 2025 U.S. Climate Report documented a slow-moving storm system that brought over 150 tornadoes to the South and Midwest, resulting in at least 24 fatalities and widespread flooding. This event underscores the increasing frequency of severe convective storms in a warming climate.(

Summaries
---------

2023–2024 as a turning point

> When our children and grandchildren look back at the history of human-made climate change, this year [2023] and next [2024] will be seen as the turning point at which the futility of governments in dealing with climate change was finally exposed.

—[James Hansen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hansen "James Hansen"), December 2023[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-Guardian_20231229-1)

Director (1981-2013) of NASA's

[Goddard Institute for Space Studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goddard_Institute_for_Space_Studies "Goddard Institute for Space Studies")

The cusp of a new era

> We are on the cusp of a new era. Fossil fuels are running out of road. The sun is rising on a clean energy age.

—[UN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") Secretary General [António Guterres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ant%C3%B3nio_Guterres "António Guterres"), 22 July 2025[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-Guardian_20250722-2)

*   May: André Corrêa do Lago, director of the [2025 United Nations Climate Change Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_United_Nations_Climate_Change_Conference "2025 United Nations Climate Change Conference") (COP30, in Brazil), said, "It is not possible to have [scientific] denialism at this stage, after everything that has happened in recent years. So there is a migration from scientific denial to a denial that economic measures against climate change can be good for the economy and for people."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-Guardian_20250528-3)
*   June: the [Energy Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_Institute "Energy Institute")'s _Statistical Review of World Energy_ suggested that 2025 may be the beginning of a [paradigm shift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paradigm_shift "Paradigm shift") in which the [energy transition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_transition "Energy transition") is driven by pursuit of [energy security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_security "Energy security") through [energy independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_independence "Energy independence") ("risk hedging" in a volatile and uncertain environment, and seeking "resilient, decentralized, and clean energy systems"), rather pursuing [climate change mitigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change_mitigation "Climate change mitigation")_per se_.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-EnergyInst_2025-4)
*   20 May: a study published in _[BioScience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BioScience "BioScience")_ said that climate change has joined [overexploitation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overexploitation "Overexploitation") and [habitat alteration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habitat_destruction "Habitat destruction"), to become a third major threat to [Earth's animals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biodiversity "Biodiversity").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-BioScience_20250520-5)

Measurements and statistics
---------------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2025_in_climate_change&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Measurements and statistics")]

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c2/1940-_January_global_average_temperature_changes.svg/250px-1940-_January_global_average_temperature_changes.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1940-_January_global_average_temperature_changes.svg)

Global average surface temperatures, shown here for each January since 1940, reached a record high temperature of 1.75°C in January 2025 despite the Earth being in a [La Niña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Ni%C3%B1o%E2%80%93Southern_Oscillation "El Niño–Southern Oscillation") (regional cooling) phase.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-Copernicus_January2025-6)

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/1978-_Global_sea_ice_extent.jpg/250px-1978-_Global_sea_ice_extent.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1978-_Global_sea_ice_extent.jpg)

Global [sea ice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_ice "Sea ice") reached a new all-time minimum in early February, and remained below the previous record of February 2023 for the rest of the month.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-Copernicus_20250305-7)

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/1750-_Radiative_forcing_-_greenhouse_gases_and_aerosols.svg/250px-1750-_Radiative_forcing_-_greenhouse_gases_and_aerosols.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1750-_Radiative_forcing_-_greenhouse_gases_and_aerosols.svg)

Hansen _et al._ (2025) wrote that the IPCC had underestimated aerosols' cooling effect, causing it to also underestimate [climate sensitivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_sensitivity "Climate sensitivity") (Earth's responsiveness to increases in greenhouse gas concentrations).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-Envt_Hanson_20250203-8) In what Hansen called a [Faustian bargain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deal_with_the_Devil "Deal with the Devil"), regulation of aerosols improved air quality, but aerosols' cooling effect became inadequate to temper the increasing warming effect of greenhouse gases—explaining unexpectedly large global warming in 2023-2024.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-Envt_Hanson_20250203-8)

[![Image 7](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/202505_Escalation_of_extreme_heat_-_247_countries_-_attribution_to_climate_change.svg/250px-202505_Escalation_of_extreme_heat_-_247_countries_-_attribution_to_climate_change.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:202505_Escalation_of_extreme_heat_-_247_countries_-_attribution_to_climate_change.svg)

Scientists in the field of [extreme event attribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extreme_event_attribution "Extreme event attribution") have concluded that in virtually all countries and territories around the world in a one-year period beginning in May 2024, human-caused global warming has increased the number of days of extreme heat events over long-term norms.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-WWA_20250530-9)

*   10 January: a summary from the [Copernicus Climate Change Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copernicus_Climate_Change_Service "Copernicus Climate Change Service") stated that 2024 was the warmest year since records began in 1850, with an [average global surface temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_surface_temperature "Global surface temperature") reaching 1.6°C above [pre-industrial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-industrial_society "Pre-industrial society") levels, surpassing for the first time the 1.5°C [warming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change") target set by the [Paris Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Agreement "Paris Agreement"). The summary also stated that 2024 was the second consecutive year with the hottest global temperature, surpassing 2023 by +0.12°C.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-10)
*   21 January: a study published in _[Nature Climate Change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature\_Climate\_Change "Nature Climate Change")_ concluded that at least 30% of the Arctic has become a net source of carbon dioxide.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-NatureCC_20250121-11)
*   28 January: a study published in _[Environmental Research Letters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental\_Research\_Letters "Environmental Research Letters")_ reported that global mean [sea surface temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_surface_temperature "Sea surface temperature") increases had more than quadrupled, from 0.06 K per decade during 1985–89 to 0.27 K per decade for 2019–23, and projected that the increase inferred over the past 40 years would likely be exceeded within the next 20 years.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-EnvRschLtrs_20250128-12)
*   3 February: a study co-authored by [James Hansen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hansen "James Hansen") published in _[Environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environment\_(magazine) "Environment (magazine)")_ concluded that the IPCC had underestimated the effect of [aerosols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerosol "Aerosol")' planet-cooling [radiative forcing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiative_forcing "Radiative forcing"), after enactment of international regulation of maritime aerosol emissions in the 2020s designed to improve air quality.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-Envt_Hanson_20250203-8) This underestimation of aerosols' effect was said to cause underestimation of [climate sensitivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_sensitivity "Climate sensitivity"), Hansen _et al._ writing that the reduction in aerosols explains the unexpectedly large global warming experienced in 2023-2024.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-Envt_Hanson_20250203-8)
*   10 February: a study published in _[Nature Climate Change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature\_Climate\_Change "Nature Climate Change")_ shows that the first single calendar year above 1.5°C relative to pre-industrial levels in 2024 indicates that most probably Earth has already entered the 20-year period that will reach the Paris Agreement limit — that is, a 20-year period with average warming of 1.5°C.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-paper-13)
*   24 February: a study published by the non-profit Initiative on GHG Accounting of War estimated that the three years of the [Russian invasion of Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "Russian invasion of Ukraine") had caused 230 MtCO 2 e (metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent) [emissions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenhouse_gas_emissions "Greenhouse gas emissions")—citing warfare, buildings reconstruction, landscape fires, damage to energy infrastructure, refugee and civil aviation displacement.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-EcoAction_20250224-14)
*   7 March: a study by [World Weather Attribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Weather_Attribution "World Weather Attribution") concluded that in a February 2025 [heat wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_wave "Heat wave"), climate change made extreme heat at least 2°C hotter and at least ten times more likely.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-WWA_20250307-15)
*   21 March: on the first World Glaciers Day (established by the UN General Assembly), the [World Meteorological Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Meteorological_Organization "World Meteorological Organization") reported that five of the past six years witnessed the most rapid glacier retreat on record, and 2022-2024 witnessed the largest three-year loss of glacier mass on record.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-WMO_20250321-16)
*   14 April: a study published in the _[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proceedings\_of\_the\_National\_Academy\_of\_Sciences\_of\_the\_United\_States\_of\_America "Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America")_ concluded that since 1940, global warming has tripled the number of days per year that the oceans experience extreme surface heat conditions, and is responsible for a 1°C increase in maximum intensity of marine heatwave events.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-PNAS_20250414-17)
*   10 May: a study published in _[AGU Advances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Geophysical\_Union#Publications "American Geophysical Union")_ said that observations from space show that Earth's [energy imbalance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth%27s_energy_budget#Energy_imbalance "Earth's energy budget") in 2023 reached values that were twice that of the best estimate from the [IPCC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intergovernmental_Panel_on_Climate_Change "Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change"), and cautioned that the ability to observe this imbalance is deteriorating because satellites are being decommissioned.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-AGUadvances_20250510-18)
*   30 May: a study jointly published by [Climate Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_Central "Climate Central"), the [Red Cross Red Crescent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Cross_Red_Crescent "Red Cross Red Crescent") Climate Centre, and [World Weather Attribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Weather_Attribution "World Weather Attribution") concluded that in the preceding year, four billion people experienced at least thirty _additional_ days of extreme heat because of climate change; and that in 195 countries and territories, climate change at least doubled the number of extreme heat days as compared to a world without climate change.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-WWA_20250530-9)
*   5 June (reported): for the first time, [NOAA's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Oceanic_and_Atmospheric_Administration "National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration")[Mauna Loa Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauna_Loa_Observatory "Mauna Loa Observatory") measured an atmospheric [carbon dioxide concentration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide_in_Earth%27s_atmosphere "Carbon dioxide in Earth's atmosphere") of over 430 parts per million.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-PhysOrg_20250605-19)
*   16 June: a study published in _[Nature Communications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature\_Communications "Nature Communications")_ found that higher temperatures (27.3°C vs. 6.4°C) were associated with a 45% higher probability of having [obstructive sleep apnea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obstructive_sleep_apnea "Obstructive sleep apnea") on a given night.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-NatureComms_20250616-20)
*   18 June: a study published in _[Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature\_(journal) "Nature (journal)")_ concluded that global warming reduces crop production by 4.4% of recommended caloric consumption for each 1°C of global warming, though adaptation measures can reduce losses.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-Nature_20250618-21)
*   7 July: a study published in _[Nature Geoscience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature\_Geoscience "Nature Geoscience")_ reported that changes in long-duration heatwaves increase nonlinearly with temperature, with increments of warming increasing the durations more than proportionately.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-NatureGeosci_20250707-22)
*   July: the [International Renewable Energy Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Renewable_Energy_Agency "International Renewable Energy Agency")'s _Renewable Power Generation Costs 2024_ said that on a [levelized cost of electricity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levelized_cost_of_electricity "Levelized cost of electricity") (LCOE) basis, 91% of new [renewable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renewable_energy "Renewable energy") utility-scale capacity delivered power at a lower cost than the cheapest new [fossil fuel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fossil_fuel "Fossil fuel")-based alternative. New onshore wind projects had an LCOE of $0.034/kWh, solar photovoltaic $0.043/kWh, and hydropower $0.057/kWh.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-IRENA_202507-23)
*   11 August: applying [extreme event attribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extreme_event_attribution "Extreme event attribution"), a study published in _[Nature Ecology & Evolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature\_Ecology\_and\_Evolution "Nature Ecology and Evolution")_ concluded that human-caused intensification of heat extremes caused a 25–38% reduction in global abundance of tropical birds from 1950 to 2020.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-NatureEcolEvol_20250811-24)
*   25 August: an article published in _[Nature Climate Change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature\_Climate\_Change "Nature Climate Change")_ reported the results of a 15-year study that concluded that long-term exposure to [heat waves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_wave "Heat wave") accelerated the aging process, with manual workers, rural residents and participants from communities with fewer air conditioners being more susceptible to health impacts.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-NatureCC_20250825-25)
*   27 August: a study published in _[Nature Climate Change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature\_Climate\_Change "Nature Climate Change")_ concluded that tropical [deforestation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deforestation "Deforestation")-induced local warming is associated with 23,610–33,560 heat-related deaths per year.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-NatureCC_20250827-26)
*   3 September: noting that the planet's [carbon sequestration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_sequestration "Carbon sequestration") capacity is not unlimited, a study published in _[Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature\_(journal) "Nature (journal)")_ concluded that fully using Earth's geologic storage capacity would help limit global warming by only 0.7°C (1.3°F).[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-Nature_20250903-27)
*   10 September: applying [extreme event attribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extreme_event_attribution "Extreme event attribution") to 213 historical heatwaves from 2000–2023, a study published in _[Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature\_(journal) "Nature (journal)")_ concluded that human-caused climate change made the median of heatwaves in 2000–2009 about 20 times more likely than a pre-industrial baseline, and heatwaves in 2010–2019 about 200 times more likely.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-Nature_20250910-28) Specifically, the study concluded that fossil fuel and cement producers enabled 16–53 heatwaves that would have been virtually impossible in a preindustrial climate.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-Nature_20250910-28)
*   10 September: a study published in _[Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature\_(journal) "Nature (journal)")_ attributed 3,400–7,400 acute deaths in North America and 37,800–90,900 chronic deaths in North America and Europe to [PM 2.5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particulate_matter "Particulate matter") (fine particulate matter) exposure from the [2023 Canadian wildfires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Canadian_wildfires "2023 Canadian wildfires").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-Nature_20250910B-29)

Natural events and phenomena
----------------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2025_in_climate_change&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Natural events and phenomena")]

*   1 January: a study published in _[Science Advances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science\_Advances "Science Advances")_ concluded that faster flow of the [Antarctic Circumpolar Current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctic_Circumpolar_Current "Antarctic Circumpolar Current") (ACC) at higher latitudes causes upwelling of isotopically light deep waters around Antarctica, likely increasing [atmospheric carbon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide_in_Earth%27s_atmosphere "Carbon dioxide in Earth's atmosphere") levels and thereby potentially constituting a critical [positive feedback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positive_feedback "Positive feedback") for future warming.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-SciAdvances_20250101-30)
*   6 January: a study published in _[Nature Climate Change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature\_Climate\_Change "Nature Climate Change")_ stated that a [fungal pathogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pathogenic_fungus "Pathogenic fungus") (_[Entomophaga maimaiga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entomophaga\_maimaiga "Entomophaga maimaiga"))_ that had successfully controlled the defoliation of the [spongy moth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lymantria_dispar "Lymantria dispar") in [North American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America") forests was becoming less effective due to climate change producing hotter, drier conditions. The study predicts this will lead to significantly decreased forest [biodiversity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biodiversity "Biodiversity") and productivity by spongy moths, evidenced by recent increases in defoliation.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-31)
*   7 January: NOAA's _[Arctic Report Card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arctic\_Report\_Card "Arctic Report Card") 2024_ reported that, including the impact of increased wildfires, the [Arctic tundra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tundra#Arctic "Tundra") region had shifted from [storing carbon in the soil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_sink "Carbon sink") to becoming a carbon dioxide [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenhouse_gas_emissions "Greenhouse gas emissions"), and that the Arctic remained a consistent source of methane—both adding to planet-warming greenhouse gases in the air.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-NOAA_20250107-32)
*   8 January: a study published in _[Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature\_(journal) "Nature (journal)")_ concluded that one-quarter of 23,496 decapod [crustaceans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crustacean "Crustacean"), fishes and [odonates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odonata "Odonata") studied, some of which provide climate change mitigation, are threatened with extinction.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-Nature_20250108-33) One-fifth of threatened freshwater species are affected by climate change and severe weather events.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-Nature_20250108-33)
*   9 January: a study published in _[Nature Reviews Earth & Environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature\_Reviews\_Earth\_%26\_Environment "Nature Reviews Earth & Environment")_ estimated that since the mid-twentieth century, global-averaged 3-month and 12-month "hydroclimate whiplash" events have increased by 31–66% and 8–31%, respectively.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-NatRvwEandE_20250109-34) Such increases amplify hazards associated with rapid swings between wet and dry states, including flash floods, wildfires, landslides and disease outbreaks.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-NatRvwEandE_20250109-34) (_Hydroclimate volatility_ refers to "sudden, large and/or frequent transitions between very dry and very wet conditions".)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-NatRvwEandE_20250109-34)
*   15 January: a study published in _[Weather](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather\_(journal) "Weather (journal)")_ reported that the terrestrial biosphere's rate of natural carbon dioxide [sequestration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_sequestration "Carbon sequestration") has fallen since its 2008 peak at a rate of 0.25% per year, a decline that will accelerate climate change.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-Weather_20250115-35)
*   21 January: a study published in the _[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proceedings\_of\_the\_National\_Academy\_of\_Sciences\_of\_the\_United\_States\_of\_America "Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America")_ reported an "abrupt, coherent, climate-driven transformation" from "blue" (more transparent) to "brown" (less transparent) states of lakes in [Greenland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland "Greenland") after a season of both record heat and rainfall drove a [state change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tipping_points_in_the_climate_system "Tipping points in the climate system") in these systems.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-PNAS_20250121-36) This change was said to alter "numerous physical, chemical, and biological lake features", and the state changes were said to be unprecedented.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-PNAS_20250121-36)
*   February (reported): though [polar bears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_bear "Polar bear") and [grizzly bears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grizzly_bear "Grizzly bear") traditionally occupy distinct habitats (marine and land), arctic warming has forced polar bears inland into grizzly bear habitats, where the two species mate to produce hybrid "[grolar bears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grizzly%E2%80%93polar_bear_hybrid "Grizzly–polar bear hybrid")" that have characteristics poorly adapted to either marine or land habitats.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-MSN_20250222-37)
*   4 February: a study published in _[Environmental Research Letters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental\_Research\_Letters "Environmental Research Letters")_ concluded that, in addition to the [2023 marine heat wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Caribbean_heat_wave "2023 Caribbean heat wave"), an extensive [river plume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_plume "River plume") caused a ~10–20 m (33–66 ft) thick strongly stratified barrier layer that contributed to [Hurricane Idalia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia "Hurricane Idalia")'s rapid intensification (Category 1 to Category 4 in less than 24 hours).[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-EnvRschLtrs_20250204-38)
*   21 February: a study published in _[npj Natural Hazards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List\_of\_Nature\_Research\_journals#npj\_series "List of Nature Research journals")_ unified studies of climatic trends and of wildland-urban interface (WUI) expansion, and concluded that climatic factors increased the frequency of high-risk fire weather by a factor of 2.5, and that the combination of climatic factors with WUI expansion led to a 4.1-fold increase in the frequency of conditions conducive to extreme-impact wildfires from 1990 to 2022 across California.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-NatHazards_20250221-39)
*   26 February: a study published in _[Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature\_(journal) "Nature (journal)")_ concluded that the [Atlantic meridional overturning circulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_meridional_overturning_circulation "Atlantic meridional overturning circulation") (AMOC) is resilient to extreme greenhouse gas and North Atlantic freshwater forcings across 34 climate models, suggesting that an AMOC collapse is unlikely in the 21st century.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-Nature_20250226-40)
*   26 February: a study published in _[Science Advances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science\_Advances "Science Advances")_ concluded that short-, mid-, and long-term ambient outdoor heat can significantly accelerate [epigenetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epigenetics "Epigenetics")[aging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ageing "Ageing") in older adults.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-SciAdvances_20250226-41)
*   5 March: a study published in _[Geophysical Research Letters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geophysical\_Research\_Letters "Geophysical Research Letters")_ concluded that redistribution of mass caused by melting of ice sheets and glaciers will shift the Earth's rotational poles from 12–27 metres (39–89 ft) by 2100, depending on the degree of future global warming.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-GeoRschLtrs_20250305-42) Changing Earth's rotational axis affects spacecraft navigation and orientation of deep space telescopes.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-GeoRschLtrs_20250305-42)
*   10 March: a study published in _[Nature Sustainability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature\_Sustainability "Nature Sustainability")_ projected that climate change's cooling of the atmosphere occupied by [space debris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_debris "Space debris") in [low Earth orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Earth_orbit "Low Earth orbit") will reduce the atmosphere's drag on the debris, extending the debris' lifetime and potentially causing a 50–66% reduction in [satellite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite "Satellite") carrying capacity at altitudes 200–1,000 km (120–620 mi).[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-NatureSust_20250311-43)
*   19 March: an article published in _[Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature\_(journal) "Nature (journal)")_ said that two major natural events occurred at the end of the last ice age: around 10,300 and 8,300 years ago, sea levels surged rapidly due to meltwater releases from the North American and Antarctic ice sheets, with peak rates of sea-level rise reaching nearly 9 mm/year — comparable to projections for the year 2100 under high-emissions scenarios.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-44)
*   25 March: an article published in _[Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature\_(journal) "Nature (journal)")_ said that volcanic eruptions over the past 603 years have significantly impacted the strength and tilt of the Atlantic jet stream, which in turn influenced extreme weather events in Europe. These jet stream shifts contributed to increased droughts when moving north and heightened flood risks when shifting south.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-45)
*   10 April: [NOAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Oceanic_and_Atmospheric_Administration "National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration") published a statement that after a few months of [La Niña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Ni%C3%B1o%E2%80%93Southern_Oscillation#La_Ni%C3%B1a_phase "El Niño–Southern Oscillation") conditions, the tropical Pacific was [ENSO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Ni%C3%B1o%E2%80%93Southern_Oscillation "El Niño–Southern Oscillation")-neutral and was likely to remain so through autumn, stating the most recent La Niña phase was very brief.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-NOAA_20250410-46)
*   21 April: NOAA confirmed the Earth was experiencing its [fourth global coral bleaching event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023%E2%80%932025_global_coral_bleaching_event "2023–2025 global coral bleaching event"), which it called the biggest to date: from 1 January 2023 to 20 April 2025, bleaching-level heat stress had impacted 83.7% of the world’s coral reef area, and mass coral bleaching had been documented in at least 83 countries and territories.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-NOAA_20250421-47)
*   30 April: a study published in _[Nature Communications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature\_Communications "Nature Communications")_ described how melting of [sea ice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_ice "Sea ice") caused by global warming allows increased areas of open water—which passes a narrower spectrum of light than the smooth continuum of frequencies passed by sea ice—to "cause major changes in both the pigment and species composition of primary producers in polar ecosystems".[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-NatureComms_20250430-48) These changes affect [photosynthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis "Photosynthesis") in ocean [phytoplankton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phytoplankton "Phytoplankton").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-NatureComms_20250430-48)
*   6 May: a study published in _[Nature Communications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature\_Communications "Nature Communications")_ concluded that [glacial melt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retreat_of_glaciers_since_1850 "Retreat of glaciers since 1850") is accelerated even when ocean temperatures are constant, a phenomenon caused when cold fresh [meltwater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meltwater "Meltwater") rushing from beneath [glaciers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glacier "Glacier") creates upward turbulence, drawing in warm ocean water from below.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-NatureComms_20250506-49)
*   8 May: NOAA's April 2025 U.S. Climate Report documented a slow-moving storm system that brought over 150 tornadoes to the South and Midwest, resulting in at least 24 fatalities and widespread flooding. This event underscores the increasing frequency of severe convective storms in a warming climate.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-50)
*   20 May: a study published in _[Communications Earth & Environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications\_Earth\_%26\_Environment "Communications Earth & Environment")_ concluded that merely maintaining a global average temperature of +1.5°C is inadequate to avoid extensive loss and damage to coastal populations in coming centuries, and hypothesized that "+1°C above pre-industrial, possibly even lower" is required to avoid such loss and damage.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-CommsEandE_20250520-51)
*   31 May: a study published in _[Communications Earth & Environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications\_Earth\_%26\_Environment "Communications Earth & Environment")_ suggested that as [glacial melt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retreat_of_glaciers_since_1850 "Retreat of glaciers since 1850") exposes soil, glacial meltwater's net sequestration of carbon dioxide gives way to water from exposed soil that enhances methane and carbon dioxide production, switching from a negative to positive warming feedback.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-NatureCommsEandE_20250531-52)
*   4 June: a study published in _[Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature\_(journal) "Nature (journal)")_ concluded that atmospheric evaporative demand (AED)—"atmospheric thirst" causing moisture to be removed from the Earth's surface—has increased [drought](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drought "Drought") severity by an average of 40% globally.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-Nature_20250604-53)
*   9 June: a study published in _[Global Change Biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global\_Change\_Biology "Global Change Biology")_ suggested that by 2020, global [ocean acidity conditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocean_acidification "Ocean acidification") had already crossed into the [uncertainty range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:PBs2023.png "File:PBs2023.png") of the [Planetary Boundary Framework](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_boundaries "Planetary boundaries").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-GlobalChangeBiology_20250609-54)
*   16 June: a study published in the _[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proceedings\_of\_the\_National\_Academy\_of\_Sciences\_of\_the\_United\_States\_of\_America "Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America")_ reported a tripling in the past half-century of the number of [planetary wave events](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rossby_wave "Rossby wave") caused by quasi-resonant amplification (QRA).[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-PNAS_20250616-55) Such wave events underlie extreme weather events such as heatwaves, flooding, wildfires, and heat dome events.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-PNAS_20250616-55)
*   7 July: findings in a study published in _[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proceedings\_of\_the\_National\_Academy\_of\_Sciences\_of\_the\_United\_States\_of\_America "Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America")_ suggested that current Earth system models overestimate the ability of [northern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Hemisphere "Northern Hemisphere")[temperate forests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperate_forest "Temperate forest") to absorb carbon, because the models do not consider the impacts of shrinking snowpack and increased soil freeze/thaw cycles.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-PNAS_20250707-56)
*   14 July: a study published in _[Communications Earth & Environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications\_Earth\_%26\_Environment "Communications Earth & Environment")_ said that accelerated East Asian reduction in aerosol emissions unmasks greenhouse gas-driven warming, enough to be a main driver of the accelerated global warming since 2010.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-CommsEandE_20250714-57)
*   5 August: a study published in _[Geophysical Research Letters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geophysical\_Research\_Letters "Geophysical Research Letters")_ concluded that a slowdown in the rate of [Arctic sea ice decline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arctic_sea_ice_decline "Arctic sea ice decline") since 2005 is largely due to natural climate variation.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-GeoRschLtr_20250805-58) The study forecast that the slowdown could continue for another five to ten years, although a faster-than-average sea ice decline would be more likely thereafter.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-GeoRschLtr_20250805-58)
*   2 September: a study published in the _[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proceedings\_of\_the\_National\_Academy\_of\_Sciences\_of\_the\_United\_States\_of\_America "Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America")_ reported that the [Gulf of Panama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Panama "Gulf of Panama")’s seasonal [upwelling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upwelling "Upwelling") failed in early 2025, breaking a >40-year record of reliability, which the researchers said "underscores how climate disruption can threaten wind-driven tropical upwelling systems".[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-PNAS_20250902-59)
*   18 September: the [World Meteorological Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Meteorological_Organization "World Meteorological Organization")'s _State of Global Water Resources Report 2024_ concluded that only one third of [river basins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drainage_basin "Drainage basin") had normal [hydrological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrology "Hydrology") conditions in 2024, and that all glacier regions lost ice for third straight year.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-WMOwater_20250918-60)

----------------------------

### Science and technology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2025_in_climate_change&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Science and technology")]

*   12 February: a study published in _[Bird Study](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird\_Study "Bird Study")_ found that [solar farms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photovoltaic_power_station "Photovoltaic power station") can benefit bird abundance and [biodiversity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biodiversity "Biodiversity") in arable-dominated landscapes, especially when managed with biodiversity in mind.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-BirdStudy_20250212-61)
*   3 March: advising policy makers to assimilate uncertainty into decision making to increase [decarbonization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change_mitigation "Climate change mitigation"), a study published in the _[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proceedings\_of\_the\_National\_Academy\_of\_Sciences\_of\_the\_United\_States\_of\_America "Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America")_ urged a "portfolio approach" of planting diverse species of trees, as that approach "reduces exposure to downside cost extremes".[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-PNAS_20250303-62)
*   May (reported): a technique involves pumping water from beneath Arctic ice and spraying it on top of the ice. It quickly refreezes, thickening the ice in that location so that it lasts longer into the warm months and increases the amount of planet-warming sunlight that is [reflected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albedo "Albedo") back into space.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-SciAm_20250520-63)
*   Spring: two Chinese companies announced battery technology to enable electric vehicles to drive hundreds of miles on a five-minute [charge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charging_station "Charging station").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-NYTimes_20250819-64)[BYD Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BYD_Company "BYD Company") developed a battery with a peak charging capacity of 1,000 kilowatts, compared to U.S. chargers with peak rates of 400 kilowatts or less.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-NYTimes_20250819-64)

### Political, economic, legal, and cultural actions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2025_in_climate_change&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Political, economic, legal, and cultural actions")]

Existential problem of planetary proportions

> (Climate change is) an existential problem of planetary proportions that imperils all forms of life and the very health of our planet. ... A complete solution to this daunting, and self-inflicted, problem requires the contribution of all fields of human knowledge, whether law, science, economics or any other.

—[International Court of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Court_of_Justice "International Court of Justice") advisory opinion[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-ICJ_20250726-65) regarding [Obligations of States in respect of climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obligations_of_States_in_respect_of_climate_change "Obligations of States in respect of climate change")

26 July 2025

*   20 January: within hours of his inauguration, U.S. President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") signed an executive order to withdraw the country from the 2015 [Paris Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Agreement "Paris Agreement"), joining Iran, Libya and Yemen as the only countries not party to the agreement.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-NYTimes_20250120-66)
*   4 March: the administration of U.S. President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") withdrew the country's representatives from the board of the United Nations' [Loss and Damage Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loss_and_Damage_Fund "Loss and Damage Fund"), which was formed to help poor and vulnerable nations cope with climate change-fueled disasters.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-Reuters_20250307-67)
*   13 March: the Costa Rica-based [Inter-American Court of Human Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inter-American_Court_of_Human_Rights "Inter-American Court of Human Rights") ordered the [Ecuadorian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecuador "Ecuador") government to protect [Indigenous people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples "Indigenous peoples") from oil operations, to leave oil in the ground underneath their lands, and to ensure future oil operations do not impact Indigenous peoples living in [voluntary isolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncontacted_peoples "Uncontacted peoples").[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-InsideClimateNews_20250313-68)
*   14 March: 440 Olympic athletes from 90 countries and 50 sports published an [open letter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_letter "Open letter") to candidates for [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_International_Olympic_Committee "President of the International Olympic Committee") of the [International Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Olympic_Committee "International Olympic Committee"), urging them to keep "the spirit of the Games alive by ensuring that sport remains accessible and safe for future generations".[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-Olympic_athletes-69)
*   24 March: the [Supreme Court of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") declined to hear the appeal in _[Juliana v. United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juliana\_v.\_United\_States "Juliana v. United States")_, ending the case in which youth plaintiffs asserted in their 2015 filing that the government had violated their [constitutional rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_right "Constitutional right") by encouraging use of fossil fuels.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-NYTimes_20250324-70) Certain other lawsuits with similar strategies were more successful.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-NYTimes_20250324-70)

[![Image 8](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ed/20201211_Billion_dollar_events_related_to_climate_change_-_U.S._-en.svg/250px-20201211_Billion_dollar_events_related_to_climate_change_-_U.S._-en.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:20201211_Billion_dollar_events_related_to_climate_change_-_U.S._-en.svg)

In May 2025, NOAA/NCEI in the Trump administration indicated that it would no longer assemble the data that forms the basis of this chart.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-Guardian_20250508-71) NOAA/NCEI has access to non-public data, so that any private databases would be more limited in scope.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-Guardian_20250508-71)

*   30 March: an [open letter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_letter "Open letter") signed by 1900 researchers called on the administration of US President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") to stop its "wholesale assault on U.S. science", including its blocking of research on climate change, and causing researchers to live in a "climate of fear" amid the administration's flagging of terms such as _climate change_ as objectionable.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-OpenLetter_20250331-72)
*   28 April: U.S. President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") dismissed the scientists and experts who compile the [National Climate Assessments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Climate_Assessment "National Climate Assessment") (NCAs) that are required by the [U.S. Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress"), the next assessment having been planned for 2028.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-NYTimes_20250428-73) Within the week, the [American Meteorological Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Meteorological_Society "American Meteorological Society") (AMS) and the [American Geophysical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Geophysical_Union "American Geophysical Union") (AGU) said that together they will produce over 29 peer-reviewed journals to cover climate change; that while not claiming they will replace the NCA, they will carry on its work.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-Guardian_20250503-74)
*   7 May: a study of [emissions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenhouse_gas_emissions "Greenhouse gas emissions")[inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_justice#Disproportionality_between_causality_and_burden "Climate justice") from 1990 to 2020 published in _[Nature Climate Change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature\_Climate\_Change "Nature Climate Change")_ concluded that two-thirds of global warming is [attributable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_justice#Disproportionality_between_causality_and_burden "Climate justice") to the wealthiest 10%, and 20% of warming is attributable to the wealthiest 1%.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-NatureCC_20250507-75) Numerous other statistics were presented.
*   8 May (reported): the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Oceanic_and_Atmospheric_Administration "National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration") (NOAA) under U.S. President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") said that NOAA's [National Centers for Environmental Information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Centers_for_Environmental_Information "National Centers for Environmental Information") would no longer update its Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters database beyond 2024, and that its information—going as far back as 1980—would be archived.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-Guardian_20250508-71)

Beyond scientific dispute

> In summary, the committee concludes that the evidence for current and future harm to human health and welfare created by human-caused [GHGs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenhouse_gas "Greenhouse gas") is beyond scientific dispute. Much of the understanding of climate change that was uncertain or tentative in 2009 is now resolved and new threats have been identified. ... The United States faces a future in which climate-induced harm continues to worsen and today’s extremes become tomorrow’s norms.

—National Academies of

Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-NASEM_20250917-76)

17 September 2025

*   30 June: the globalchange.gov website of the [U.S. Global Change Research Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Global_Change_Research_Program "U.S. Global Change Research Program"), established in 1990 to host legislatively mandated reports including the [National Climate Assessments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Climate_Assessment "National Climate Assessment"), was taken down by the [Trump administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "Second presidency of Donald Trump").[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_climate_change#cite_note-NYTimes_20250701-77)
